items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations Reading Time: 3 minutes A global soil restoration movement, launched through a 30,000-kilometer motorcycle journey, has reached an estimated 4 billion people and is pushing nations toward policies that protect agricultural soil from irreversible degradation. Save Soil , the movement behind this global push, centers on a stark warning: soil with insufficient organic content essentially turns to sand, triggering cascading consequences for food security, water systems, biodiversity, and climate stability. Currently, 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are classified as degraded, a figure that underscores the urgency behind what has become one of the largest environmental awareness campaigns in recent history. The soil restoration movement was founded by Indian yogi and environmental activist Sadhguru, who embarked on a 100-day motorcycle journey spanning 27 countries and 30,000 kilometers from the United Kingdom to India to raise awareness. That journey became the foundation for a campaign claiming to have reached 4 billion people, roughly 60% of the world’s electorate, through 691 events and interviews, more than 8,970 media stories, and 50 iconic landmarks illuminated worldwide in support of the cause. At the core of the soil restoration movement is a specific, measurable goal: restoring at least 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil by shading land and enriching it with plant litter and animal waste. The movement outlines a three-pronged policy strategy presented at the UN Convention to Combat Desertification’s COP15: incentivizing farmers to increase soil organic matter, making carbon credits more accessible to farming communities, and establishing preferential marketing for produce grown in healthier, higher-organic-matter soil. The soil restoration movement aims to restore 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil, which can hold up to 90% of its weight in water, addressing a crisis in which 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are already degraded. Photo by Tom Fisk on Pexels. The stakes extend across multiple interconnected crises. Degraded soils cannot adequately absorb and regulate water flows, contributing to droughts and floods alike, while organic-rich soil can hold up to 90% of its weight in water and release it gradually over time. Soil also stores roughly three times more carbon than living plants and twice as much as the atmosphere, meaning continued degradation risks releasing roughly 850 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, more than three decades of combined global emissions. The soil restoration movement has secured formal commitments from national governments through Soil Health memoranda of understanding, with countries including Azerbaijan, Romania, Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Suriname, Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guyana, and the United Arab Emirates signing agreements committing to policies restoring and safeguarding soil health. The Caribbean region, in particular, has shown unified support, with multiple island nations joining within the same campaign cycle. Across North America, the soil restoration movement gained traction at the municipal level, with more than 150 cities proclaiming March 21 as Save Soil Day, including Washington, D.C., Austin, San Diego, Baltimore, Philadelphia, Phoenix, and dozens of smaller municipalities across the United States and Canada. These proclamations, while largely symbolic, reflect growing local government engagement with soil health as a civic priority rather than a purely agricultural concern. International institutions have also voiced support. The United Nations Environment Programme, the Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Health Organization, the World Food Programme, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature have all publicly backed the soil restoration movement’s objectives, alongside the Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture and the Commonwealth of Nations. The campaign explicitly compares itself to a previous global environmental success story: the 1987 Montreal Protocol, through which 197 countries agreed to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals after confirming the Antarctic ozone hole. That agreement eliminated 99% of ozone-depleting substances, and current projections suggest the ozone layer will fully recover by mid-century. The soil restoration movement positions this precedent as proof that coordinated international policy can reverse seemingly intractable environmental crises when sufficient public and governmental will exists. Beyond policy advocacy, the soil restoration movement has catalogued more than 1,000 sustainable soil management solutions spanning 193 nations, alongside engaging younger generations directly, with 3 million children reportedly writing letters to their national leaders advocating for soil health policies. Recent reporting connected to the movement has also highlighted soil degradation’s role as a driver of global migration, with projections suggesting human displacement could double by the century’s end as soil degradation, climate change, and food insecurity compound one another. Land-related conflicts have already played a significant role in most major wars across Africa since 1990, underscoring how soil health intersects with geopolitical stability far beyond agricultural productivity alone. As the soil restoration movement continues expanding its policy reach, its core argument remains consistent: thriving soil policies require public support, and public support requires sustained awareness. Whether this translates into a binding international framework like the one that reversed ozone depletion remains to be seen, but the scale of global engagement so far suggests soil health has moved from a niche agricultural concern to a mainstream environmental and public health priority. The post Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM California just gave apartment renters a shot at solar. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a bill legalizing plug-in solar panels, also called balcony solar, clearing the way for a technology that doesn’t require a roof you own, a contractor, or tens of thousands of dollars up front. Compliant models are expected to hit shelves in mid-2027. How the hardware works The hardware is minimal: a few small panels, an inverter, and cables. The panels can hang from a balcony railing, mount outside a window, or sit in a backyard. Existing models run from $300 to $2,200 , much cheaper than a rooftop installation because you set them up yourself. In Germany , where they’re already common, you just plug them into a wall outlet. California’s version has more certification requirements for now, but that’s where the law is pointed. Who is historically left out of rooftop solar? Rooftop solar has always had prerequisites. You need to own your home, have a qualifying roof, and either have capital or qualify for financing. That locked out renters from day one, along with a lot of low-income households and anyone in a multifamily building. “These small, easy-to-use solar panels will give everyone, including renters, the relief they desperately need on our outrageous energy bills,” said state Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote the bill. It passed with bipartisan support. The benefits of plug-in A plug-in system can cover up to 20 percent of a home’s electricity needs and save as much as $500 a year for a small apartment. California electric bills have climbed hard over the past few years, so that number means something to a lot of people. The registration overhaul The registration change matters nearly as much as the legalization. Under the old rules, adding a plug-in panel meant completing the same interconnection paperwork required for a full rooftop system, which could cost up to $800 and take days. Advocates noted that process cost more than the panels themselves in some cases. Under the new law, registration is free and immediate. Systems must stay under 1,200 watts per home, pass third-party safety certification, and include protection against backfeeding electricity into the grid during outages. Products currently on the market don’t meet those standards yet, so the old registration process still applies for now. The sale of non-compliant systems becomes illegal in 2030, and the law runs from 2027 to January 1, 2030. “The market is sending a clear signal to manufacturers that they need to develop a California system,” said Cora Stryker, co-founder of Bright Saver, a plug-in solar advocacy group. California is the tenth state to pass this kind of law. Utah went first in March 2025; Colorado, Virginia, and Maine followed. But California is the country’s largest electricity market, which means manufacturers pay attention in a different way. What advocates have been describing for years, plug-in solar on the shelf at a hardware store, is now a reasonable near-term prospect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Italian federation of pediatricians designed a box of games to help parents ask their kids how their day went. Let’s think about this for a minute. A medical organization had to build a conversation starter for families at dinner because something else kept stealing away everyone’s attention. Fifteen restaurants across Sardinia are running a one-month pilot called A tavola senza schermi , “at the table without screens.” Families who come in are asked to put their phones away. In exchange, staff hand over a “reunion kit,” a pediatrician-designed box with games, drawings, and prompts for parents and kids to work through together. The thinking behind the program The scheme is the work of Anna Cau, Sardinia’s children’s ombudsman, a former juvenile magistrate who partnered with the island’s restaurant federation to make it happen. The 15 restaurants joined voluntarily. Ultimately, the plan is to expand on the same basis. Cau is deliberate about how she describes the initiative. “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others,” she said. The usual framing for children’s screen time puts the entirety of the problem on parents: their choices, their habits , their failures, their job to fix. Cau is coming at this issue from a different, more holistic angle. She wants the places families actually move through to be part of the answer rather than indifferent to the question. What restaurant owners notice Emanuele Frongia, president of the Sardinian restaurant federation, described what pushed the conversation forward. Families come in and sit down together, but within a few minutes, the talking stops. “We increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices,” he said. “Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.” It’s that last part that we really need to sit with and consider. The phone at the family table isn’t always something a kid reaches for. In fact, sometimes it’s a parent who puts it in their hands. The table in Italy isn’t just where you eat. It’s where the work of being a family gets done: the catching up, the arguing, the unremarkable talking that makes people feel known to each other. What Cau and the restaurant owners around her are watching is that shift happening meal by meal, as the phone becomes easier to reach for than whatever the silence might turn into. The real power of the reunion kit The reunion kit is both the sweetest part of this initiative and the most honest. It’s a concession that stepping away from screens needs a little structure to start. Most families handed a box of games by a waiter will end up talking without consulting the instructions. The box matters because without it, the phones inevitably come back out, at least for now. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: In an Oct. 28 letter from the editors , Life Magazine — which was founded in 1936 and became an icon of visual storytelling — announced it will begin publishing again after nearly 20 years. Its first new print issue “offers a window into an America searching for meaning.” That 250-page edition hits newsstands Nov. 23, The New York Times reported , the inaugural step forward in a revival made possible by Bedford Media’s acquisition of the publication in 2024. The holding company was founded the year prior by model Karlie Kloss and is co-owned by her husband, venture capitalist Joshua Kushner. More than 120 people put together the forthcoming issue, focusing on “finding the ordinary in the extraordinary, and the extraordinary in the ordinary,” per the editors’ letter. The reincarnated brand will expand into other avenues as well, amplifying its quarterly print pieces through digital storytelling, documentaries, and events. © CORBIS—Corbis/Getty Images When Henry Luce founded Life , at the tail end of the Great Depression and three years before World War II began, the intent was to “harness the emerging power of photojournalism,” the letter reads. Luce had co-created Time magazine 13 years prior to deliver a concise weekly news digest to busy readers. Life took an opposite approach, inviting Americans to pore over dramatic multi-page photo spreads and essays that told stories about 20th-century topics large and small: from groundbreaking science and civil rights to movie stars and the lives of everyday people. The first issue came out Nov. 23, 1936 ( you can scroll through it in its entirety online ). The cover story captured one of the major public works projects in development under then-President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s historic New Deal, and Page 2 featured a photo of a baby held upside down by a doctor moments after birth. RELATED: Gordon Parks: How Life Magazine’s First Black Staff Photographer Shed Light on Social Justice With Expressive Images That view into the miracle of life (no pun intended) likely felt unprecedented to readers at the time. The newborn was George Story, who went on to become a journalist and liked to joke at parties that a nude picture of him had once been published in a national magazine. Santi Visalli/Getty Images After nearly four decades, Time Inc. ceased weekly publication of Life in 1972, citing production costs. The magazine returned in 1978 as a monthly publication and ran until 2000. In a full-circle moment, its final issue in that format also featured Story — this time covering his death at age 63. It was resurrected again in 2004 as a weekly newspaper supplement, but shut down three years later due to a decline in newspaper readership and ad sales, the company said, per NBC News. The upcoming revival marks exactly 90 years since Life began. Take a look back at some of its most iconic photos and covers. Ήταν μια μικρή ομολογία, αλλά έφερε το βάρος μιας επιδημίας. Σε όλες τις πανεπιστημιουπόλεις των ΗΠΑ,…
items.descriptionOriginal: Somewhere between the gorges and botanic gardens of Cornell University's campus, a student on a guided nature walk looked up from hours of screen time and said something that stopped the walk leader cold: "This is the first time I've actually touched grass." It was a small confession, but it carried the weight of an epidemic. Across U.S. campuses, colleges are turning to "social prescribing" -- a practice borrowed from the UK where physicians write actual referrals, logged in electronic health records, for time in nature, art, movement, or community -- as a complement to counseling and medication for the surging mental health crisis among students. At Cornell, over 2,200 students received nature prescriptions last year, and 88 percent reported an improved mood. At Stanford, a dedicated care navigator connects students to pottery classes, dance workshops, and live performances -- and 80 percent of those who attended reported better mental health. What these programs are quietly surfacing is something older than any diagnosis: that belonging, beauty, and the sensory world are not luxuries but medicine. The student who finally touched grass wasn't being dramatic. She was describing a kind of return.

items.descriptionOriginal: Do you tend to experience jealousy, have difficulty trusting people, or resist emotional intimacy out of fear? While genetics can play a role in qualities like these presenting themselves, they may also be explained by attachment theory: the idea that our earliest relationships influence how we’ll connect with people later in life. “As children, we build our understanding of relationships based on our caregivers,” Jennifer Rolnick , a licensed clinical psychologist and co-owner of Watch Hill Therapy, told Nice News. “If a caregiver is consistently supportive, a child learns that relationships are safe. If a caregiver is inconsistent, distant, or intimidating, a child learns defense mechanisms in order to survive.” These early, deeply ingrained patterns shape how we read people, manage conflict, and regulate emotions, resulting in specific “attachment styles” that we hold onto into adulthood, Rolnick explained. Those of us with a secure attachment style usually find it easier to nurture and sustain close connections, while those with insecure attachment styles (avoidant, anxious, or disorganized) often have trouble in adult relationships. But the good news is that it’s entirely possible to change your patterns. We spoke to Rolnick and three other experts to help us understand the four attachment styles, including how they develop and what you can do to form more secure relationship habits with friends, family, and romantic partners moving forward. Understanding the 4 Attachment Styles Avoidant We might develop an avoidant attachment style if our primary caregiver was emotionally distant or dismissive, per Utah State University . This attachment style can also occur if we were regularly and unreasonably depended on or criticized as a child, Hider Shaaban , a licensed clinical psychologist and founding executive director of Philadelphia Center for Psychotherapy, told Nice News. “So [they] may develop a core belief of ‘If I let people get close to me, they will drain me, judge me, and maybe even hurt me along the way, so it’s safer that I keep my distance.’” Adults with avoidant attachment styles prioritize independence and self-reliance over close connection, added Terri DiMatteo , a licensed professional counselor at Open Door Therapy. “Deep emotional intimacy or vulnerability feels uncomfortable to them,” she said. “When a romantic or non-romantic person gets too close, they are likely to pull away and create distance. Avoidantly attached adults have great difficulty expressing their own emotions, and in the back of their mind is the refrain ‘I don’t need anyone. I am good on my own.’” fizkes—iStock/Getty Images Plus According to the Cleveland Clinic , other potential signs of avoidant attachment include: A strong sense of independence Difficulty trusting people Avoiding physical or emotional intimacy Feeling uncomfortable when people try to get close Being dismissive of others Commitment issues Anxious If you had an inconsistent or emotionally unpredictable caregiver, you might have developed an anxious attachment style, explained Emily Bly , a licensed clinical psychologist and CEO of Psychology Partners Group. When parents “are particularly inconsistent in their emotional responses — vacillating between warm and connected at some moments and cold, nonresponsive, and detached in other moments — [it] can result in the child internalizing a sense that they are ‘not good enough’ or to blame in some way.” Bly added that people with anxious attachment styles tend to fear abandonment and worry that a loved one could withdraw their affection at any time and without warning. They frequently seek reassurance and have trouble believing that people really care for them, and are often on high alert for potential signs of dismissal or rejection. For instance, they might interpret a partner’s subtle shift in tone or a friend’s delayed text response as a signal that something is wrong in the relationship. According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of anxious attachment include: Feeling unworthy of love Difficulty spending time alone High sensitivity to criticism Jealous tendencies Low self-esteem Trouble trusting people Fear of abandonment or rejection Disorganized A disorganized attachment style (also known as fearful avoidant) can occur if a primary caregiver is dangerous or violent. If a parent consistently frightens a child, the child has nowhere to turn in times of distress, Bly explained. As a result, they may develop a “freeze” response to emotional turmoil, feeling that they can’t escape or rely upon their parent. In adulthood, they may shut down and “quasi-dissociate” when stressed, making it difficult for someone else to reach them emotionally, she continued. Relationships can therefore be confusing, as it may feel like the fearful avoidant-attached person has one foot on the gas and another on the brakes. Igor Suka—E+/Getty Images “A person with disorganized attachment craves security and attachment like anyone else, but the fear embedded in this longing will sometimes put the person in a state of ‘system overload,’” Bly said, “where they might be more likely to disappear or ‘ghost’ the attachment figure who tries to get too close to them.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of disorganized attachment include: Difficulty trusting others Trouble with emotional regulation Fear of rejection Confusing, contradictory behaviors Other traits of anxious and avoidant attachments Secure When caregivers provide consistent predictability, abundant love, clear expectations, and straightforward communication, children are often more likely to develop secure attachments. “Basically, they will start to develop the belief system that ‘relationships are generally safe,’ which will help them establish connections with others without the worry of being rejected,” Shaaban said. When they do experience rejection, he added, they’re less likely to take it personally and can bounce back more quickly. People with secure attachment typically view themselves and others positively, communicate honestly and openly, and find it easier to build and maintain lasting, healthy bonds, according to Utah State University. DiMatteo agreed: “Securely attached relationships are safe, relaxed, reliable, and supportive, allowing each person to be their authentic self, knowing they are accepted and valued as they are.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of secure attachment include: Finding it easy to trust others Effective communication Emotional regulation Feeling comfortable spending time alone Finding it easy to connect with others Healthy conflict resolution Being emotionally available to other people How to Become More Secure If you’re prone to forming avoidant, anxious, or disorganized attachments, you can develop an “earned secure” attachment style through healthy adult relationships, positive life experiences, and working with a therapist, per the Cleveland Clinic . Seeing a mental health professional experienced in attachment theory and relationships is especially important if you have a history of trauma, Shaaban noted. You can also try the following to develop healthier, more secure relationship patterns. Understand Your Story: Think about your early childhood and how you developed an insecure attachment style, Bly said. Recognize that your caregiver’s faults, such as inconsistency or emotional distance, reflect their own struggles and have nothing to do with you. With that knowledge, you can begin to rewrite your internal narrative and develop a healthier view of yourself and other people. Seek Out Stable, Secure Relationships: “Be purposeful about seeking out and establishing connections with people who are emotionally mature, consistent, and grounded,” DiMatteo advised. Observing and interacting with securely attached people — including friends, a romantic partner, or a therapist — can help you understand what healthy relationship patterns look like, aiding you in eventually adopting similar behaviors. andreswd—E+/Getty Images Identify Your Triggers: Note the situations that activate your emotional defense mechanisms. “Track your thoughts, bodily sensations, and immediate coping mechanisms when triggered,” Rolnick said. “Writing down your patterns helps you understand yourself rather than running on autopilot.” Practice Honest, Open Communication: Secure attachment involves clear, direct, and authentic interactions with others, and Rolnick suggests working on this by sharing a vulnerable feeling or need with someone you trust once a week. “Vulnerability means something different for every person, and it’s important to gently push your window of tolerance. You might say ‘I felt anxious when I didn’t hear back from you for a few days,’ or ‘I’m having a hard day and feeling anxious — can we talk?’ Each time you face your fear directly, you build your ability to handle similar challenges in the future.” RELATED: Dealing With a Difficult Relationship? Here’s How Psychology Says You Can Shift the Dynamic

Η θεματοφύλακας που κουβαλούσε ιδιωτικά την αίσθηση της αποτυχίας ήταν, για όλους γύρω της, η ζωντανή καρδιά του Aubrey Indepe…
items.descriptionOriginal: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton swept floors, bought supplies for children who couldn't afford them, and turned smiles "up instead of down" -- work she once measured against a college degree she never earned and found herself wanting. The custodian who privately carried a sense of failure was, to everyone around her, the living heart of Aubrey Independent School District in Texas. When the superintendent called her to the podium under the pretense of a routine meeting, Hampton unrolled a small red carpet and found her own name printed on it: Marilyn Hampton Elementary School. The next day, she was still crying. "Whoever thought a janitor would have a school named after them," she said, and in that sentence lives the quiet revelation the story holds: that a life spent in faithful, unglamorous service to others can quietly become the most significant thing in a room, in a district, in a community's memory -- long before anyone thinks to say so out loud.

items.title: Τι κάνει τη Scary Music Scary; Ο συνθέτης "Obsession" για τη δημιουργία μιας ταινίας τρόμου δολοφονίας
items.titleOriginal: What Makes Scary Music Scary? The “Obsession” Composer on Crafting a Killer Horror Movie Score

items.descriptionOriginal: In the second half of Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining , there’s an iconic sequence that’s arguably as terrifying as Jack Nicholson’s ax-wielding rampage. It begins quietly, the camera following Shelley Duvall as she walks toward a shadowy room. Her footsteps echo in the silence before an ominous sound creeps in, almost like distorted white noise. The music builds, getting louder and more complex as warped high notes slowly penetrate the din. It’s chaotic, dissonant, deafening, mirroring the emotions on Duvall’s face, until finally, finally — well, we won’t give you any spoilers . “If you watched it on mute, I don’t know if it would feel nearly as scary,” Rock Burwell told Nice News of the classic flick. Burwell composed the score for this year’s breakout indie horror film, Obsession , which raked in $500 million-plus off a $750,000 budget, making it the highest-grossing movie ever produced for under $1 million. The Los Angeles-based composer recognizes how essential music is to evoking emotion in filmgoers, and his eerie orchestration played an outsize role in Obsession’s success. “What just generally has always drawn me to music in the first place is its ability to influence how we feel,” he said. But what exactly makes scary music scary? We may all have some general idea of the characteristics of creepy music — the crescendo of staccato strings in Psycho ’s shower scene comes to mind — but the way in which a score achieves its effect varies greatly. There are certain common elements, however, that lend themselves to disconcerting an audience. Subverting Expectations For Obsession , Burwell — after discussions with writer-director Curry Barker — chose a nontraditional approach, opting to subtly discomfit viewers through dreamy, nostalgic melodies, slightly pitch-bending his notes and drenching everything in reverb. “It was fun to explore not coming in with these really harsh, interval, screechy-sounding kind of things that you hear in a lot of horror movies,” he explained, “but actually coming from something that feels a bit more warm and almost comforting. But the way it moves and is undulating underneath is very — it kind of gets under your skin a little bit more.” Composer Katy Jarzebowski , who recently scored the award-winning documentary Gaslit featuring Jane Fonda, has been working in the industry for over 20 years. She noted that today’s savvy audiences are well-versed in the language of film. The key to unsettling them, then, is to present a musical choice they don’t necessarily understand or expect. “If you give them something that they know and love, then it kind of takes that feeling of discomfort away,” she explained, adding: “[When filmmakers] don’t give them something that they expect, it becomes uncomfortable.” Tension Tension is the heart of any horror film, and a good one typically leaves viewers on tenterhooks throughout. To that end, Burwell noted that the descending melodies and drawn-out cues he used can cause audiences to feel as though they’re suspended, waiting for a resolution that never comes. “Everything is very, like, ambient and long, and it’s slow moving,” he said. “I think that the pace of it really allows those feelings to sit in a bit longer.” He added that he’s heard from fans that the sweet-yet-tainted score had them feeling “very comforted, but at the same time, feeling kind of bad or that there’s something missing or that there’s yearning.” Jarzebowski agreed with the idea of holding out on viewers. “It’s a lot about where you choose to come in or where you choose to hold back,” she said. “You know, a lot of times [it’s] not giving that kind of pillow for the audience to land on to remind them that they’re in a movie in the first place.” In the Studio Pete Horner is an Emmy-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer at Skywalker Sound (who also happens to be married to Jarzebowski). He pointed out that the terror conveyed through a horror movie’s sound isn’t merely from the music itself. Foley is the art of creating sound effects in a studio — things like footsteps or a door creaking — and Horner said it can be used to great effect for inducing fear in quiet scenes. “By accentuating those things, it kind of draws you closer to the action, and it makes you feel uncomfortable because you shouldn’t be able to hear that,” he explained, adding: “It mimics what happens when you are scared, which is that you become hyperaware of your surroundings. And when you’re not scared, you probably don’t hear the footsteps at all, even though they are happening in the space you’re in. But if you are scared, every little tiny sound has huge meaning.” Additionally, gradually removing the ambient background noise (called “room tone”) from a scene can be extremely disconcerting. “It’s something you want to use sparingly in a movie, but if you pull out of all of the ambiences, the effect that it has is the audience will hold their breath,” Horner said. “Because they’re listening, they’re trying to hear into the sound, and there’s nothing there. And it’s a very scary feeling.” Working With the Cinematography It’s typical for musicians to score to picture, meaning they create the music as they watch the film. But sometimes, the two arts inform each other more equally. In Obsession , Burwell sent early cues to Barker while he and director of photography Taylor Clemons were coming up with the shot list. Barker later told Burwell that playing the music on set really helped establish the mood they were going for. Likewise, watching Clemons’ claustrophobic cinematography influenced Burwell’s choices for the score. “We kind of leaned on the darkness, like, there’s not much high frequency information in the music, and there’s not a whole lot of light in a lot of these scenes, too,” Burwell said. “I’ve kind of referred to it as a lot of the score feeling like a lead blanket or something like that. Like, it’s just really heavy. And I think the cinematography really informed that for me.” Experimentation Starting with what’s considered the first-ever horror flick (a three-minute silent French film from 1896 titled The Haunted Castle ) to the dozens coming out in 2027 , the genre is a confirmed favorite of moviegoers. Call it sublimation or call it masochism, but people like to be scared. And that means composers have ample opportunity — and one could say the imperative — to get creative. “Horror is a great place for composers, especially to experiment with different things because a lot of times, you’re trying to create a fear that someone doesn’t know yet,” Jarzebowski said, adding: “We already have Psycho , we have Stranger Things , we have [horror filmmaker and composer John] Carpenter — all this horror language that we’ve created. So you already know what to be scared of. So there’s always room for, like, ‘OK, what else can we do to make it even scarier? What haven’t they heard yet?’”

items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.description: Οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν ότι ο εμβολιασμός μητέρων ποντικών μεταφέρει αντισώματα που προστατεύουν τα ευάλωτα νεογνά έναντι της Klebsiella pneumoniae. Η Klebsiella pneumoniae είναι ένα επικίνδυνο βακτήριο που σκοτώνει χιλιάδες βρέφη σε χώρες χαμηλού και μεσαίου εισοδήματος κάθε χρόνο και είναι ο μεγαλύτερος δολοφόνος παιδιών παγκοσμίως. Τέτοιες λοιμώξεις μπορεί να είναι δύσκολες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered that vaccinating mouse mothers transfers antibodies that defend vulnerable newborns against Klebsiella pneumoniae . Klebsiella pneumoniae is a dangerous bacterium that kills thousands of infants in low- and middle-income countries each year and is the leading killer of children globally. Such infections can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium’s growing resistance to antibiotics and there is currently no vaccine available to prevent infection. The study in Science Advances points to a promising new strategy for protecting vulnerable infants from the drug-resistant superbug by harnessing maternal immunity. “ Klebsiella pneumoniae is a serious threat to newborns who have not yet developed their own immune defenses,” says the study’s senior author, David A. Rosen, an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Our study shows that maternal immunization can effectively bridge that critical window of vulnerability, giving newborns the protection they need right from birth.” K. pneumoniae is a big problem around the world, especially in the hospital where it can cause pneumonia and other infections among adults and children. In low- and middle-income countries, where children often get exposed to the bacterium in their environment, it drives severe bacterial blood infections, known as sepsis. Because K. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to standard antibiotics, doctors are often left without effective medicines to treat such infections. The Rosen team collaborated with the lab of Drew Schwartz, an assistant professor of pediatrics, to model K. pneumoniae sepsis in newborn mice that mimics the infection seen in children and asked if vaccinating a pregnant mouse would prevent infection in pups. Female mice were immunized at the time of mating and then again once or twice during pregnancy. The vaccine targets two of the most dangerous types of K. pneumoniae —known as K1 and K2—and was developed by Omniose, a St. Louis-based startup. Rosen had previously published findings that show the vaccine is effective in preventing K. pneumoniae infection in adult mice that can progress to life-threatening liver, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and other infections. Two weeks after birth, the young mice were exposed to lethal doses of the bacteria, either the K1 or K2 type. Of the two-week-old mouse pups from unvaccinated mothers, 0% infected with the K1 type and less than 35% with the K2 type survived. In contrast, of the young mice from vaccinated mothers, more than 80% infected with either type survived. Whether the mother received two or three doses of the vaccine did not impact survival. The researchers drew blood weekly from the young mice starting on their day of birth and continuing up to six weeks of life. They also collected breast milk from lactating mice. They found high concentrations of vaccine-specific antibodies in both the milk of vaccinated mothers and their newborn mice over the course of the study. “Mice that were never immunized themselves are highly protected from a lethal infection just from the durable antibodies transferred to them from their mother,” explains first author Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab. The researchers are now testing updated vaccines designed to shield against multiple strains of the superbug found across the globe. “This study presents the first evidence that giving moms a vaccine could be an effective strategy for protecting their babies against these severe infections,” says Rosen. “And it also has established a practical model that we can now use to test therapies and vaccines that will bring us one step closer to human clinical trials with the ultimate goal of impacting global health.” This work was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Gates Foundation, and the Washington University Department of Pediatrics. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official view of the NIH, the Gates Foundation or other funders. Competing Interest Statement: Robinson LS, Darwech I, Knoot CJ, and Harding CM have a financial stake in Omniose, a for-profit entity developing bioconjugate vaccines using patented technology reflected in the data presented in this and other published manuscripts. Source: Washington University in St. Louis The post Can a vaccine for moms protect infants from a deadly superbug? appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A teenager built a supply distribution network where families request what they need without filling out any forms or declaring themselves as someone in need. She also added a program that researches each family’s cultural background and sends handmade crafts alongside the package. That’s Vivian Ho, the first nominated Local Changemaker in The Optimist Daily’s new series. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including six countries that just put a dollar figure on their EV investments, a Columbia University finding on the minimum movement needed to offset a desk job, and what pest experts actually recommend instead of vinegar. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Karissa: Hi, everyone. I’m Karissa. Arielle: I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: So good to be back this week. It’s feeling very spooky over here. How about you, Karissa? Karissa: Super spooky and Halloweeny as we prepare for the holiday over the weekend, and a time change over in the US. I know over in Amsterdam, you’re already having those darker evenings. Arielle: Yes, we had our time change last weekend, and yeah, it does get dark so early, and it feels quite wintry, but that’s all right. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I miss the sun. I know. Maybe a week of this weather and I’ll be longing for the sun, but there is no shortage of good news to brighten your day at The Optimist Daily. Arielle: No, especially because we started publishing our Local Changemakers series this week on Wednesday. You can look forward to one Local Changemaker feature every Wednesday in the run-up to Thanksgiving. This week was a little bit different. We have two features because we have the Student Maker story, which kind of inspired us to highlight younger changemakers this year, and then the first nominated Local Changemaker. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I can’t wait to dive into them. But before we do- Mm … that, we wanna remind you that all these solutions are available in our newsletter format, whether you want that every day or just a weekly digest. It’s free to sign up, and the link to do that is in the show notes. Arielle: If you’re more of a social media feed type of news consumer, then you can follow us on all social platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are, @OdeToOptimism. You can also reach me and Karissa directly by emailing us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We really love getting comments, questions, feedback, or anecdotes that you wanna share with us. So yeah, feel free to shoot us an email whenever. Karissa: We also encourage you to share with friends, loved ones, all this positive news from The Optimist Daily, and remind them that, you know, good things are happening out there in the world. As usual, a big thank you to our Emissaries who financially support the mission of The Optimist Daily. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is also in the show notes. With all of that said and done, shall we jump into the spooky solutions of the week? Let’s get into it. Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician Karissa: The first solution is “Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician”. This piece is informed by an actual pediatrician about how to make Halloween work for every kid in your family, and the framing is really specific to each age group in a way that’s genuinely useful. For toddlers, one tip that I thought stood out was to bring a wagon, even if your kid insists they don’t need one when you’re trick-or-treating or attending some kind of Halloween event. For school-aged kids, uh, Dr. Kristen Cook, who is the pediatrician that gives all this advice in the article, frames Halloween as giving earned independence when you’re trick-or-treating, so you can, you know, hang back a couple houses, let the kids lead, but keep them in sight. And then when it comes to teenagers, they might be going to Halloween parties, and at these parties they can come across some peer pressuring situations. It’s good to talk to them about an exit plan for situations they might not be comfortable with and discuss how to deal with these potentially uncomfortable situations, but ultimately trusting them to handle it the right way. So lots of good tips here. This just brings so much Halloween nostalgia back for me. Arielle: Yeah, I, um… my parents didn’t let me participate in Halloween growing up. I know. Heartbreak. I think it just was, uh, you know, we are an immigrant family coming from a very Christian country- Yes, yeah … and they kind of saw it as, like, kind of like devil worship. But, you know, we got over that stage. I was already, um… I kinda aged out of Halloween, uh, in the traditional sense where you go trick-or-treating and all of that. But my youngest sister was able to participate, and she had, like, really fun costumes. As a little kid, she wanted to be a tissue box one year. Um- That’s a good one … which was really weird. It was, like, a High School Musical tissue box, because we had like, High School Musical, um, wrapping paper. And so that’s how she decided to dress up. Karissa: I love it. Arielle: Yeah, so I have vicarious Halloween memories through my youngest sister. Karissa: Well, I mean, as an adult now, maybe you can do some, some of this stuff. NYC food pantries are stocking pet food for struggling households Karissa: The next solution is very heartwarming, and it’s that “New York City food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households”. New York State just put $500,000 towards making sure pet owners don’t have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their animals. There are now 22 food pantries across all five boroughs stocking free pet food, and the reason this program exists is kind of heartbreaking and kind of sweet at the same time. The story mentions a woman named Cassandra in Brooklyn who sometimes eats less so her Shih Tzu doesn’t go hungry, and she’s far from alone. The demand for pet food grew after SNAP benefit cuts, which tells you a lot about just how far those cuts reach into people’s lives. Animal welfare groups have known for years that financial hardship and pet surrender are directly linked, but this program is essentially trying to catch families before they hit that wall. 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk Karissa: The next solution is a health lifestyle related one, and it’s “Five research backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk”. Columbia University researchers ran a study trying to find the minimum effective dose of movement to counteract sitting all day. The answer was actually surprisingly specific. It’s simply five minutes of walking every 30 minutes that makes a difference. NPR actually then tested that with 20,000 of their listeners and found the exact same thing. So this article breaks down that finding plus four other fixes. Arielle, have you ever heard of this tip to walk five minutes every 30 minutes? Arielle: No, but to increase focus, I use the Pomodoro Technique, which is when you set the timer for about 20- 25 minutes and then give yourself a five-minute break. Because I work from home- Yeah … I am always kind of hunched over my laptop. So that is a trick that I use, and I do generally get up and, like, walk around the house. Um- Yeah … so I guess my body intuitively knew that this was a good thing to do, but it’s nice to have the science back it up. Karissa: The whole concept of this kind of, like, movement snack, um, short burst of activity is catching fire and a good suggestion. I guess I’ll mention one more thing about this solution, but you can check out the rest on optimistdaily.com. The whole posture section of this article talks about how the idea of sitting up straight and holding it advice is actually not correct. The actual physical therapist guidance is that your best posture is your next posture, meaning any fixed position causes strain eventually. New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries Karissa: Well, the next solution is “New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries”. NJ Transit has been installing art exhibitions at train and bus stations since 2019, and the program just expanded to its eighth location. The new show is about railroads and 250 years of American history, which is a pretty fun yet informative thing to encounter while you’re just trying to catch your train, the history about railroads. But the whole premise of this is that transit spaces are great for public art because nobody goes there expecting to see any. The encounter is accidental, which makes it different from an intentional gallery visit. I really like this, um, rise of art in public spaces, and it kind of reminds me of a solution we shared a couple months ago about how over in Warsaw they’re putting libraries in commuter stations. So if you have a little time, a layover in transportation, you can go check out the library. So I think this is a really cool kind of global trend. Arielle: And it’s really nice that the program actually pays the artists stipends because public art rarely comes with a real budget, and a lot of the time public art is like a, a mural that maybe someone painted for free or graffiti, which honestly, I’m a huge fan of graffiti. Some of the tags are really impressive, and some of them- Yeah … are just kind of silly, but they’re entertaining in their own way. Um, but that obviously doesn’t come with payment. If anything, it might come with a fine. Karissa: Right. Exactly. In this broader conversation about what public spaces are for, whether that’s a transit station, a library, park, you know, it can be a lot more than just something that people move through. Student Makers: bringing free STEM to students on three continents Karissa: Moving on to the Changemaker series, we talked more about Student Makers in this deeper dive. They are a group bringing free STEM to students on three continents. And like Arielle mentioned, this is the story that made us decide to make the entire series this year about people under 30, because young people are really just doing so many impressive things to change the world. At Student Makers, former students become the instructors. It’s often high schoolers teaching middle schoolers, and the founder’s whole argument is that it’s more relatable to have, um, you know, people who are closer in age to you to help teach things than an adult expert teaching the same material. Like we mentioned, we’ll have some of the main players behind Student Makers on the podcast in the beginning of 2027, which is crazy to even say that 2027 is around the corner. But we look forward to welcoming them on and hearing directly from them. Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity Arielle: I will take over from here, Karissa, and my first solution is actually the first nominated changemaker for this series. The title- Ooh … of the article is “Meet Vivian Ho, the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity”. Most programs that distribute supplies to low-income families ask that family to identify themselves before they get anything. So basically, you have to fill out a form, you check a box, you explain your situation to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built her nonprofit, All the Same organization, around removing that whole process. Families request what they need anonymously, and nobody has to declare themselves as someone in need to get the help they need. And she started this at just 16, which is quite impressive. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: The anonymous sign-up system is what makes this really special. Vivian’s read on situations like this was that the stigma of asking for help was keeping families from asking at all. So she just said, “Let’s get rid of that.” There’s also something within this nonprofit. There’s another, uh, initiative called the Cultural Surprises program, and it’s something I hadn’t seen before. So volunteers research the cultural background of the family they’re packing for, and handmade crafts reflecting that culture go out alongside the supply package, and it turns a resource delivery into something more like recognition, something that makes that family feel really seen. I’m not gonna get into all of the details, but I do encourage people who are interested in learning more about Vivian Ho and perhaps how to support her work to check out the article because it is really, really remarkable that she was able to do this as a teenager. Karissa: Congratulations to Vivian for being nominated by two of The Optimist Daily community members who are involved with the project as well, a nomination from her co-founder and a volunteer that she inspired to start his own project nominated Vivian. So go check that out if you wanna learn more. Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems Arielle: The next solution is titled “Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems”. Kenya just signed a $160 million deal to protect nearly 67,000 square miles of some of the most important wildlife habitat in Africa, including the Maasai Mara and Tsavo. But the interesting part isn’t just the money, it’s the structure of how that money gets released, because this isn’t a grant that arrives and then disappears. So the funding mechanism is called Project Finance for Permanence. Money flows in tied to specific government policy benchmarks, and not all the money gets, uh, given upfront, let’s say. If Kenya doesn’t hit the milestones, then those funds never get released. Tsavo holds 40% of Kenya’s elephants and 20% of its critically endangered black rhinos, and that’s just to give you an idea of what’s at stake for wildlife and geographically. Kenya committed to the global 30 by 30 target and was sitting at about 20% to 23% coverage, so this deal would largely close that gap by 2030. Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works Arielle: The next solution is titled, “Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works.” So every fall, people reach for the vinegar bottle as a first line of pest defense. They spray the windows, they spray the door frames, and then it feels like they’ve done something. But two pest control experts basically say, “You’ve done nothing.” The reason why is in this article, and there’s also one fall tip in here that’s actually kind of strange and useful. So vinegar unfortunately only kills soft-bodied insects on direct wet contact, and then once it dries, then the vinegar doesn’t really do anything against cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. And researchers found negligible effects on most common household insects. What really works is, like, caulking windows and weather-stripping doors and adding door sweeps. That will actually stop bugs from getting in. Spraying is just treating the symptom and not really addressing the entry point of where all of these pests try to come in and get cozy ’cause the weather outside is getting worse. Um- Yeah … and then the, the weird tip, well, I found it weird or unexpected, is the acorn tip. If you are bringing acorns or pine cones inside this fall, then you should put them in 150-degree Fahrenheit oven for about 30 minutes first, and that will kill whatever’s living inside them, and then you can, like, decorate your home for the holidays in peace knowing that there’s no hidden critter in your pine cone just waiting to make your house their home. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: The DIY home pest control has surged since the pandemic. People want low-chemical solutions, and that’s why I think vinegar gets so much reach. But yeah, unfortunately it’s just not as effective as everyone thought it was. Karissa: Well, it’s good to know so we don’t waste our vinegar and our time. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Karissa: I- I have to say, though, maybe this is bad, but I do like to use just the harsh chemicals and get them out of the way- … if they do come in the house. So I, I don’t hesitate to use the big stuff. Arielle: Yeah. It’s… You know, we appreciate your honesty here. I’m sure there are a lot of listeners who struggle with pests and are like, “Yeah, I’m just gonna obliterate.” The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs Arielle: The next solution is titled, “The seven best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs”. Most of the list made sense to me, but there’s one of them that takes three years before it really starts producing, and both experts say plant it anyway. And yeah, there are pretty good reasons, which I will get into. So first, herbs are the economic winner here. They’re among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store. You usually buy more than you use, and growing them means you harvest exactly what you need when you need it. The strange one was the asparagus. It takes two to three years of establishment before you get a real harvest, so you really have to be committed to the asparagus, and also you have to like asparagus. I like asparagus, but I know a lot of people aren’t the biggest fans. But a well-maintained bed produces for up to 20 years. One expert calls it something you’ll have basically for life. Both experts are clear that the garden only saves money if you plant what your household actually eats. So start with vegetables you already go through the most, and that will help you save money in the end. How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility Arielle: The last solution that we are gonna share with everyone this week is titled “How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility”. So there is that conflict in Iran that has been driving oil prices up 33% this year. But six European countries collectively avoided nearly $2.2 billion in oil import costs just because they have enough EVs on the road. That’s not a projection or a goal, that’s an actual number from a six-month window. Denmark alone displaced 13% of its entire 2025 oil consumption. So there’s a real dollar security argument for EV adoption here that goes beyond anything to do with the environment, although the environment is very important. Karissa: Yes. Arielle: Hopefully this, uh, this will encourage other economies to really invest in their EV development, but also hopefully this conflict ends soon. Karissa: Yeah. So- For multiple reasons, of course. But it just goes to show how moving towards renewable energy, sustainable energy across the board is just the best path towards energy security. Arielle: Definitely. Well, those were all of the solutions we had this week, but before we go, we have a positive quote. We will both be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, have a great weekend. items.descriptionOriginal: Food accounts for a third of humanity’s greenhouse emissions. And sure enough, the most carbon-gushing foods are also the ones that tend to be the worst for our health, such as meats and dairy. So what if we tried taxing that carbon, to nudge people toward higher-plant diets that are healthier for people and planet alike? A new study in Nature Food explores how these food emissions taxes could be applied to countries around the world with different levels of wealth and greenhouse emissions. It shows how they could be tweaked to manage the delicate interplay between food prices, poverty, hunger, and health—while still cutting billions of tons of annual emissions. Economists have estimated that growing populations and increasing meat consumption worldwide could cause the environmental footprint of our food—including greenhouse emissions— to balloon by 50 to 90 percent by 2050 . This has spurred recommendations that humanity shift its diet , toward fewer animals and more plants. Emissions taxes paid by consumers buying foods are one way to encourage a shift away from meats, dairy, eggs , and sugars . But questions remain about how those taxes can be applied fairly to countries around the world—given that wealthier nations have more ability to pay them, and that many of these same nations also contributed disproportionately to rising greenhouse gases in the first place. In the new study, researchers used economic, trade, and public health models to predict how well different types of taxes would curb greenhouse emissions—and also, how they would impact food prices They compared two tax scenarios. In one, emissions are priced the same worldwide, at a constant cost of USD$ 185 per metric ton of CO 2 equivalent (tCO 2 eq). In this system, wealthy countries would still pay more taxes, because their food systems emit more tons of CO 2 . In the other system, the cost-per-ton of emissions is scaled up or down, based on each country’s wealth—thereby further increasing the taxes paid by consumers in wealthy countries (to as much as $969 per tCO 2 eq), while reducing those paid by lower-wealth countries (to as little as $21 per tCO 2 eq). The researchers compared these two scenarios both with and without a second provision, in which governments would also subsidize fruits and vegetables to further lower the prices that consumers pay for these low-carbon foods. Their results suggest that taxes based on a fixed-price-per-ton would reduce food-related emissions most sharply—by up to 18.7 percent, or about 2.6 billion tCO 2 eq worldwide each year. But such taxes would likely worsen overall health in some countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam—even after accounting for reductions in heart disease and diabetes—because they might make food less affordable to some people, compromising nutrition. The authors found that adjusting the price-per-ton of emissions based on national wealth would lessen this problem. And subsidizing the cost of fruits and vegetables would further decrease it. Together these two tweaks slightly reduced the emissions that were prevented—but they were still predicted to cut worldwide food emissions by 17 percent, or about 2.3 billion tCO 2 eq per year. The authors recommended that these efforts to reduce the negative impacts on the poor could be further explored, with detailed studies of poverty in individual countries, and potentially by excluding some critical sustenance foods such as fish or rice from the taxes in some countries. Bouyssou, et al. “ Food emissions taxes can deliver health and environmental benefits with limited leakage .” Nature Food , 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? Reading Time: 2 minutes In September 2026, solar developer D3 Energy installed a large solar array, not on land or on a rooftop, but on the surface of a reservoir that serves the water needs of the village of Monroeville, Ohio. This floating power plant covers 12 acres of the reservoir’s 16 acres. If a solar facility of this size, which contains 9,220 solar panels, were built on dry land, it would require 30 acres. So doing it the Monroeville way helps to keep open land available for farming, housing, business or industry, conservation land, or any other use. This 6-megawatt installation is projected to generate about 7,500 megawatt-hours of clean electricity to this village of 1,300 residents. Monroeville has already operated a 4-megawatt ground-mounted solar array, built in 2017. This 10-megawatt total gives the town roughly 13 times as much solar-generated power per capita as the rest of Ohio. Their floating solar array is among the five largest in the U.S. In addition to the clean power produced and the avoidance of using land that might be put toward other needed uses, Floato-voltaics projects such as this one have several other benefits. First, the physical barrier created by the floating platforms significantly reduces water evaporation by blocking direct solar radiation and intercepting wind blowing across the water’s surface. Solar “on the water” thereby reduces evaporation by 30% to 80%, depending on temperatures and humidity in the immediate area. The result, depending upon the size of the floating power plant, is an annual savings of millions of gallons of valuable drinking and irrigation water. Beyond clean power, floating solar arrays like Monroeville’s reduce reservoir water evaporation by 30% to 80% by blocking direct solar radiation and wind, saving millions of gallons of drinking and irrigation water annually. Photo courtesy of D3 Energy . Second, by depriving the water of sunlight, there is a sizable reduction of toxic algal blooms. Photosynthetic organisms like blue-green algae require sunlight to thrive. By heavily shading parts of the reservoir, the concentrations of floating solar panels limit the light penetration needed for massive algal blooms. This naturally improves water quality, reducing expenses from chemical treatments needed to purify the water. Third, more fish. During the warmer months, the floating platforms insulate the reservoir’s water against seasonal temperature spikes, helping support cold-water fish species. Local reservoirs are often favorite local fishing spots. And fourth, cleaning issues. Land-based solar arrays, whether in farming or more urbanized areas, often deal with dust, dirt, and other airborne debris. For best panel performance, cleaning of their surfaces in these situations is advisable. Open bodies of water are inherently less affected by blowing dirt and dust, keeping the panels cleaner longer and reducing maintenance costs. All things considered, with all the bodies of fresh water dotting the planet, maybe we should all look more closely for floato-voltaic opportunities just beyond our own backyard.
